questions.prompt: Per Lesson 1, a SOC's mission is described as three verbs that function as one pipeline rather than three separate jobs. Which option correctly names that three-verb pipeline, in order?
options: Monitor, detect, respond
Detect, monitor, alert
Prevent, detect, recover
Collect, correlate, contain
questions.explain: Lesson 1 defines the SOC's mission as one pipeline: monitoring produces the visibility a SOC needs, detection turns that visibility into a signal worth attention, and response is the action taken once the signal is confirmed. The lesson's 2 a.m. laptop example shows all three steps firing in exactly that order.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps two of the three real verbs but puts them in the wrong order and swaps in 'alert' for 'respond' — Lesson 1 is explicit that monitoring has to come first to produce the visibility detection depends on, and the mission's third verb is the actual response action (like isolating the laptop), not merely raising an alert.

questions.prompt: Match each role from Lesson 2 to what it's actually responsible for.
right: Monitors the alert queue, does initial investigation, and decides whether to close or hand off an alert
Takes handed-off alerts, uses broader access and tooling to confirm real incidents, and performs containment
Proactively hunts for compromise that never triggered a rule, and tunes the detection tooling itself
Handing an alert or incident to the next tier when it exceeds the current tier's access, tooling, or certainty
questions.explain: Lesson 2 lays out a strict division of labor: Tier 1 triages the queue and escalates when something exceeds its access or certainty, Tier 2 takes that escalation and has the broader access to confirm and contain a real incident, and Tier 3 doesn't wait for alerts at all — it hunts proactively and tunes the rules Tier 1 and Tier 2 rely on.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 3's ________ coverage model hands the alert queue off between SOCs in different time zones, such as the Americas, EMEA, and APAC, so no single office has to staff an overnight shift.
questions.explain: Follow-the-sun coverage is Lesson 3's term for the model where each regional SOC works its own normal daytime hours and hands off open alerts and context to the next region as its day ends, producing a continuous relay around the clock without any office working through its own night.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about reactive versus proactive SOCs, per Lesson 4.
options: A purely reactive SOC only investigates and responds to alerts as correlation rules raise them
A slow, deliberate data exfiltration that stays under every rule's threshold would be missed indefinitely by a purely reactive SOC
Threat hunting is the one proactive practice from Lesson 4 that doesn't depend on an alert firing in the first place
Most real SOCs flip from fully reactive to fully proactive in a single, well-defined step
Metrics-driven management means tracking numbers like MTTD and MTTR to confirm objectively whether the SOC is actually improving
questions.explain: Lesson 4 defines a reactive SOC as purely alert-driven, which is exactly why a slow exfiltration that never crosses a rule's threshold goes unnoticed indefinitely — nothing ever fires to put it in front of an analyst. Threat hunting is the proactive practice that would actually surface it, since it doesn't wait on an alert. Metrics-driven management is the third proactive practice, tracking MTTD/MTTR so the SOC knows objectively whether it's improving. Maturity isn't a single flip — Lesson 4 is explicit that proactive practices get layered onto the reactive baseline gradually, not switched on all at once.

questions.prompt: A firewall logs a port scan from an external IP address. Minutes later, an endpoint agent behind that same firewall logs an antivirus alert. Per Lesson 5, which SIEM function is specifically what ties these two separate, individually-dismissible log entries into one incident?
options: Correlation
Centralization
Retention
Alerting
questions.explain: Lesson 5 uses this exact port-scan-plus-antivirus-alert example to show correlation at work: centralization just gets both log entries into one place, but it's the correlation engine that ties them together by source IP and timing into a single incident — the pattern a human watching either log alone would never catch.

questions.prompt: Put these three steps of the SIEM pipeline from Lesson 6 in the order they actually have to run.
items: Aggregation: pull logs from firewalls, servers, endpoints, and applications into one central system
Normalization: map each vendor's differently-formatted fields into one shared schema
Correlation: combine the now-comparable events across sources to detect a pattern
questions.explain: Lesson 6 is explicit that this pipeline has to run in exactly this order: you can't correlate logs that are still in a dozen incompatible vendor formats, because a correlation rule looking for 'source IP' has to find a field by that name in every log it compares — which is exactly what normalization guarantees before correlation ever runs.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a SIEM from a plain log management tool, per Lesson 7?
options: A SIEM adds continuous, automatic correlation and alerting on top of log management's centralize-and-search foundation, while log management only acts when a human searches it
A SIEM and a log management tool are functionally identical; the only difference is marketing
Log management performs real-time correlation, while a SIEM only stores logs for later search
A SIEM is simply a log management tool with a longer data retention period
questions.explain: Lesson 7's test is functional, not semantic: log management centralizes and lets someone search logs, but it waits to be asked — nothing happens until a human looks. A SIEM starts from that same foundation and adds correlation rules that run continuously and automatically, plus alerting that fires the moment a rule trips, without anyone searching first.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C reverses the actual capabilities entirely — Lesson 7 is explicit that log management has no built-in, continuous correlation; it's the SIEM that correlates in real time and alerts automatically. Swapping which category does the automatic correlating is precisely the kind of misunderstanding the lesson warns against when job postings or vendors blur the line.

questions.prompt: Match each SIEM platform from Lesson 8 to what it's actually known for.
right: Long-standing enterprise platform built around its own search language, SPL
Cloud-native SIEM built on Azure, queried with KQL, tightly integrated with Microsoft 365 Defender
Open-source-rooted platform (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Beats, Kibana) usable as general log analytics or, with an add-on, as a full SIEM
Known for a correlation engine that groups related events into a single consolidated 'offense'
questions.explain: Lesson 8 ties each platform to one defining trait: Splunk to SPL, Sentinel to KQL and the Azure/Defender ecosystem this path goes deep on next, QRadar to its 'offense' grouping, and the Elastic Stack to its open-source roots and flexible self-hosted-or-cloud deployment.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank, using the PRI calculation from Lesson 9: a syslog line's priority value is calculated as facility times 8 plus severity. For the line below, facility 4 (auth) and severity 2 (Critical) produce a PRI value of ________.
questions.code: <34>Oct 28 10:15:32 firewall01 sshd[1234]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.55 port 51413 ssh2
questions.explain: Lesson 9 walks through this exact line: facility 4 (the auth/security facility) times 8 is 32, plus severity 2 (Critical) equals 34 — the <34> a SIEM's syslog parser reads before it has parsed a single word of the actual message text.

questions.prompt: A SOC pushes a WEF subscription to thousands of branch-office machines at once via Group Policy, with each machine then forwarding matching events on its own. Per Lesson 10, which subscription model is this?
options: Source-initiated (push)
Collector-initiated (pull)
Agent-based collection
Agentless API polling
questions.explain: Lesson 10 names this exact pattern — a GPO pushing the subscription configuration out to hundreds or thousands of machines, each one then forwarding matching events on its own — as source-initiated (push) subscription, the common choice at scale. Collector-initiated flips that: the collector itself maintains the source list and reaches out to pull from each one, which suits smaller, more tightly controlled sets of machines.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about agent-based versus agentless log collection, per Lesson 11.
options: A well-configured agent can buffer events locally if the connection to the SIEM drops, and send them once connectivity returns
Agentless collection is often the only practical option for a firewall or switch that has no supported way to run third-party software
Agent-based collection has zero overhead on the host it's installed on
Most SOCs standardize on one approach for every device type rather than mixing both
Agentless collection carries real risk of missed events if the polling interval is too wide or connectivity drops during a burst of activity
questions.explain: Lesson 11 is explicit that a well-configured agent's local buffering is its real strength during an outage, and that agentless collection is often the only option for appliances that can't run third-party software — but it also carries real risk when a polling interval is too wide or the link drops during a burst. Agents do have real overhead (CPU, memory, deployment, updates) rather than zero, and the lesson's actual recommendation is a mix chosen per device type, not standardizing on one approach everywhere.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 12, mapping differently-named fields from different log sources — like a firewall's src_ip versus a Windows event's SourceAddress — into one common field name the whole platform uses is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 12 defines normalization as mapping differently-named fields from different sources into one common field name, often against a published schema like Splunk's Common Information Model or Microsoft Sentinel's ASIM — without it, a correlation rule written against src_ip would quietly miss events from a source that logged the same value under a different field name.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a SIEM correlation rule from a network IDS signature, per Lesson 13?
options: A signature matches a single packet or payload pattern in isolation the moment it's seen, while a correlation rule reasons across multiple events and across time, often from more than one log source
A correlation rule and an IDS signature are the same mechanism, just running on different hardware
An IDS signature requires a time window to function, while a correlation rule never does
A correlation rule only ever examines a single log source, while a signature examines several at once
questions.explain: Lesson 13 draws this distinction directly: a signature answers 'does this one thing look malicious?' by matching a single packet or payload the instant it's seen, while a correlation rule answers 'does this sequence of otherwise-normal-looking things add up to something malicious?' by reasoning across multiple events, across time, often pulled from more than one log source.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D gets the actual source-count relationship backwards — it's the correlation rule that typically draws from more than one log source (a Windows authentication log here, a VPN log there), while a single IDS signature matches one packet or payload in isolation. Reversing which tool spans multiple sources is exactly the mix-up Lesson 13 is written to prevent.

questions.code:
RULE: Brute-force logon followed by success
SOURCE: Windows Security Event Log (Logon events)
GROUP BY: source IP

IF   count(event = "logon failure", group) >= 5
     WITHIN time_window = 10 minutes
AND  event = "logon success" occurs for the same group
     WITHIN the same 10-minute window, after the failures
THEN alert(severity = high, title = "Possible brute-force login success")
questions.prompt: This rule groups by source IP instead of by user account, on a network where hundreds of employees share the same VPN gateway's exit IP. Per Lesson 14, what's the real problem with this grouping key?
options: Failures and successes from completely unrelated users sharing that exit IP would get treated as one coherent brute-force pattern, when they're actually unrelated events
The rule would no longer have a time window at all
Grouping by source IP makes the rule run slower than grouping by user account
The rule would stop detecting any brute-force activity whatsoever
questions.explain: Lesson 14 is explicit that the grouping key is what ties individual events together into one coherent story — getting it wrong, like grouping by source IP instead of by account on a shared VPN gateway, means five unrelated employees' failed logins plus one unrelated employee's successful login get treated as a single attack pattern, which is exactly backwards from what the rule is supposed to catch.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about tuning a correlation rule, per Lesson 15.
options: A brand-new correlation rule almost always fires more than expected in its first days live against a real production environment
Adding an exclusion for a known-benign backup service account is a better fix than raising the threshold for every account
Alert fatigue from an untuned rule is only an annoyance, not a genuine security risk
Tuning a rule once at launch is sufficient; well-tuned rules never need revisiting
An analyst who has dismissed the same false positive forty times is measurably more likely to give the forty-first alert from that rule a quick glance instead of a real investigation
questions.explain: Lesson 15 is explicit that new rules are noisy by default against messier real environments, and that a targeted exclusion for a specific known-benign source (the backup account) is the better fix over a blanket threshold change that would also miss real attacks. It also treats alert fatigue as a genuine security risk, not a mere annoyance, because a dismissed-forty-times pattern measurably dulls an analyst's attention on the forty-first alert. Tuning is explicitly ongoing, not one-time — new accounts and changing schedules make a rule noisy again later.

questions.prompt: For the lateral-movement use case in Lesson 16, the correlation logic groups by user account and counts distinct destination hosts authenticated to within an hour, rather than just counting total authentication events for that account. Why?
options: Counting only total authentication events would also flag a normal user who logs into the same one or two systems repeatedly, missing the real signal of one account suddenly reaching many different hosts fast
Distinct host counting is required because Windows logs cannot record the same user authenticating twice in one hour
Total authentication events and distinct host counts always produce an identical number
Grouping by user account was deprecated in favor of grouping by destination host
questions.explain: Lesson 16's use-case development process traces lateral movement to its actual signal: the same account authenticating to an unusual number of distinct hosts in a short window, faster and wider than that account's normal baseline. Counting raw authentication events instead would conflate a normal user's repeated logins to the same one or two systems with a real attacker spreading across many different hosts — exactly the distinction distinct-host counting is built to catch.

questions.prompt: A correlation rule fires on 'admin login from a new geographic location.' The analyst confirms the login really did come from a new country, at the stated time, from the named account — and an IT ticket confirms the admin is traveling for a conference. Per Lesson 17, which of the three triage outcomes is this?
options: Benign true positive
False positive
True positive requiring escalation
Invalid alert
questions.explain: Lesson 17 uses this exact example to define a benign true positive: the alert is accurate — the login really happened exactly as described — but the activity itself turns out to be legitimate, not malicious. That's different from a false positive, where the activity didn't happen the way the rule assumed at all.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about validation, scoping, and escalation, per Lesson 18.
options: A correlation rule's alert text is a summary, not a guarantee that the activity happened the way the rule assumed
Scoping means checking what else — other hosts, accounts, systems — might be touched by the same activity
An alert that's validated as malicious but fully scoped and within Tier 1's authority to contain still must be escalated to Tier 2 automatically
An alert genuinely needs escalation when it's confirmed malicious beyond Tier 1's authority, the scope is unclear, or it needs deeper tools Tier 1 doesn't have
Skipping validation and trusting an alert's label at face value can cause an analyst to close a real true positive or escalate a false positive
questions.explain: Lesson 18 defines validation as checking the raw data behind an alert's claim, scoping as figuring out what else is affected, and lists exactly three escalation criteria: confirmed malicious beyond Tier 1's authority, unclear scope, or needing deeper tools. It's explicit that an alert meeting none of those — validated, malicious, but fully scoped and within Tier 1's own authority — gets handled and documented at Tier 1, not escalated automatically.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 19, a real investigation case note must cover five things every time — what happened, what was checked, what was found, what action was taken, and ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 19 lists timestamps as the fifth required element of a case note — when the alert fired, when it was reviewed, and when the action was taken — alongside what happened, what was checked, what was found, and what action was taken. Leaving any one of the five out, the lesson says, stops the note from doing its job.

questions.prompt: Match each escalation channel from Lesson 20 to what it actually is.
right: The default path for most escalations — case note and evidence attached to a ticket routed to the Tier 2 queue
A phone call, page, or shared incident-channel message used alongside a ticket when something can't wait
Using a case's severity level to decide whether it rides the normal queue, triggers an immediate page, or both
An escalation that hands Tier 2 the classification, scope, evidence, and a clear reason, so they don't redo Tier 1's work
questions.explain: Lesson 20 defines each channel distinctly: a ticketing system is the default path, a direct handoff supplements it for urgent cases, severity-based routing decides which path a case takes, and a clean handoff is the standard all of this exists to meet — classification, scope, evidence, and a clear reason, so Tier 2 doesn't have to re-validate from scratch.

questions.prompt: A SOC manager wants to add a panel showing 'total alerts processed since the SIEM went live' to the main analyst dashboard. Per Lesson 21, what's the real problem with that panel?
options: It's a vanity metric — true and measurable, but it doesn't tell an analyst what to act on in the next five minutes, the dashboard's actual job
Lifetime totals are mathematically impossible for a SIEM to calculate accurately
That panel would violate the compliance retention requirements covered in Chapter 2
Analysts are not permitted to view any historical totals under SOC policy
questions.explain: Lesson 21 is explicit that a dashboard is not a report — almost everything on it should answer 'does this need a human to act on it right now?' A lifetime total like events processed since go-live is exactly the vanity-metric example the lesson uses: true and impressive-looking, but it never changes what an analyst does next, which is what crowds out the open-alerts and queue-depth panels that actually matter.

questions.code:
Correlation rule fires: 2:47 PM
Attacker's first malicious login (found in log review): 1:15 PM
Escalated to Tier 2: 2:55 PM
Account disabled, host isolated: 3:40 PM
questions.prompt: Using Lesson 22's worked example and the timestamps above, MTTD for this incident is ________ minutes (2:47 PM minus 1:15 PM).
questions.explain: Lesson 22 walks through this exact timestamp set: MTTD measures the gap between when the attack actually started (1:15 PM, reconstructed from log evidence) and when the SOC first noticed it (2:47 PM, when the correlation rule fired) — a 92-minute gap, which is the attacker's dwell time for this incident.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about workload metrics and leadership reporting, per Lessons 23-24.
options: A rising alerts-per-analyst number combined with a shrinking average time spent per alert usually means analysts are rushing, not that triage got easier
A report like 'parsed 1.2 billion events, fired 3,814 alerts' is technically accurate and tells leadership exactly what they need to decide on
A growing backlog carried over to the next shift is a sign staffing hasn't matched incoming volume
Good executive reporting reframes the same real data around business risk and trend, rather than inventing new numbers
A specific ask like 'headcount at current staffing can't sustain this workload past Q3' is a request leadership can actually evaluate
questions.explain: Lesson 23 ties rising alerts-per-analyst with shrinking time-per-alert to analysts rushing, and a growing backlog to understaffed volume. Lesson 24 is explicit that a wall of raw operational statistics is accurate but tells leadership almost nothing about risk reduction or investment need — good reporting reframes the same real numbers (true positives blocked, the MTTD trend) around business risk, and pairs it with a specific, evaluable ask like a headcount request tied to the workload trend.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym SOAR stand for, and what does the 'Response' word specifically add that a SIEM alone, per Lesson 25, does not?
options: Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response — Response means the platform can carry out an actual action itself, like blocking a sender or isolating a host, rather than only alerting and waiting for a human
Security Operations, Automation, and Remediation — Remediation means logging an incident for a later audit
Security Orchestration, Analysis, and Reporting — Reporting means generating the leadership summaries from Chapter 6
Security Orchestration, Automation, and Recovery — Recovery means restoring a system from backup after an incident
questions.explain: Lesson 25 spells out SOAR as Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response, and is explicit that Response is the piece separating it from a SIEM: a SIEM detects and alerts, then waits for a human, while a SOAR playbook can actually block a sender, quarantine a file, or isolate a host itself the moment its conditions are met.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D gets the acronym's third word and its meaning both wrong — Lesson 25 defines the 'R' in SOAR as Response (taking a real action like a block or quarantine), not Recovery, and restoring from backup is never described as what separates SOAR from a SIEM anywhere in the lesson.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 26, a scenario is only a good candidate to turn into a SOAR ________ if it's both repeatable and well-understood — every reasonable outcome and the correct response to it already known in advance.
questions.explain: Lesson 26 defines a playbook as a defined, automated sequence of steps triggered by a specific alert type, and is explicit that it only works for scenarios that are repeatable (common enough to be worth automating) and well-understood (every branch of the decision tree already known) — a genuinely novel incident fails both tests and has no pre-agreed decision tree to follow.

questions.prompt: Select every category of work that Lesson 27 says still requires a human analyst, even in a SOC with mature SOAR playbooks.
options: A novel attack pattern that doesn't cleanly match any known category
An ambiguous alert, like an executive logging in from an unusual location at 2 a.m., that needs business context a tool can't know
Building, testing, and tuning the playbooks themselves
Extracting a sender address and URL out of a routine phishing report
Final sign-off on a high-stakes action, like terminating an employee's access, with serious consequences
questions.explain: Lesson 27 lists novel attack patterns, ambiguous alerts needing business context, playbook building/testing/tuning, playbook exceptions, and final accountability for high-stakes actions as the real categories that still need a human. Extracting a sender address and URL from a routine phishing report is exactly the opposite — it's the pure automation example from Lesson 26 that SOAR was built to take off an analyst's plate.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 28's worked phishing-report playbook in the order they actually run.
items: Ingest: the forwarded email lands in the phishing-report mailbox and the SOAR platform picks it up as a new case
Extract: the playbook pulls the sender address, link text, and any attachments out of the email automatically
Enrich: the playbook checks the sender address and URL against threat intelligence feeds
Branch and respond: if confirmed malicious, auto-quarantine the email and block the domain at the gateway
Notify: an analyst is told what happened, on either branch, even the one requiring no human decision
questions.explain: Lesson 28 walks this exact sequence: ingest (orchestration connecting to the mailbox), extract (pure automation pulling out indicators), enrich (checking threat intel for a verdict), branch and respond (the actual quarantine/block action once a verdict exists), and notify, which happens on both branches so a human stays in the loop even when the platform needed no judgment call to act.

questions.prompt: Alert B (Director of Sales logging in from Lisbon) and Alert C (accounts-payable clerk logging in from Chicago, then Hanoi 39 minutes later) both start with a 'new location' signal, and both turn out to be true positives. Per Lesson 29, what specific piece of scoping information separates Jordan closing one as benign and escalating the other immediately?
options: Alert C showed impossible travel distance/time plus a hidden mailbox rule forwarding invoice-related mail externally, while Alert B's login matched an approved travel request with no further suspicious activity
Alert C's account had a higher job title than Alert B's account
Alert B's login used a stronger password than Alert C's
Alert C occurred during business hours, while Alert B occurred overnight
questions.explain: Lesson 29 is explicit that both alerts share the same 'new location' trigger, but Jordan's scoping step finds completely different context: Alert B's travel matches an approved request with no other unusual activity, so it closes as a benign true positive, while Alert C's 39-minute Chicago-to-Hanoi gap is physically impossible travel, compounded by a hidden inbox rule forwarding invoice and wire-related mail externally seconds later — meeting every one of Chapter 5's escalation criteria at once.

questions.prompt: Match each chapter to the specific piece of Lesson 31's full-shift case it supplied.
right: Windows Event Forwarding and the mail platform's audit log delivering the two raw login records into the SIEM
The standing impossible-travel rule that grouped the two logins by user ID and raised one composite alert instead of two separate low-priority ones
Jordan running validate-scope-classify and writing a full case note before escalating to Tier 2
The containment playbook that ran disable-account, revoke-sessions, delete-rule, and post-summary in under three minutes once Sam confirmed the compromise
questions.explain: Lesson 31 traces the business-email-compromise case through each supplying chapter in order: Chapter 3's collection pipeline delivers the raw login records, Chapter 4's correlation rule turns them into one composite alert, Chapter 5's triage process is what Jordan runs before escalating, and Chapter 7's SOAR playbook executes the already-confirmed containment actions in under three minutes instead of the roughly 40 minutes an earlier similar case took by hand.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 30's impossible-travel correlation rule build in the correct order.
items: Define the triggering event as any successful authentication from a monitored sign-in source
Group matching events by user_id and require at least two distinct countries within a 60-minute window
Calculate the required travel speed between the two login locations and raise an alert if it exceeds 500 mph
Add an exception for known corporate VPN exit-node ranges before shipping the rule live
questions.explain: Lesson 30 builds the rule in exactly this order: first defining what event to even watch (successful authentication), then grouping by identity within a correlation window so a single login can never be impossible on its own, then calculating a required travel speed instead of guessing at a country list, and only then tuning in the VPN exit-node exception — skipping straight to deployment without that last tuning step is what would flag Thornfield's own legitimate VPN traffic as an attack.
